source.title: Can Structured Templates Facilitate LLMs in Tackling Harder Tasks? : An Exploration of Scaling Laws by Difficulty
source.authors: Zhichao Yang; Zhaoxin Fan; Gen Li; Yuanze Hu; Xinyu Wang; Ye Qiu; Xin Wang; Yifan Sun; Wenjun Wu

record.file_problem: No apparent garbling or truncation; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports that increasing the amount of low-difficulty synthetic fine-tuning data can reduce downstream math accuracy, and argues that data difficulty matters. This refines the broad claim that performance improves with scale, but it does not test the original pretraining-loss laws.
record.gate_note: The relevant results measure AIME24 accuracy against synthetic fine-tuning data volume and compare a smaller, curated Open-R1 dataset with the synthetic data. The paper does not measure held-out cross-entropy loss, sweep parameters or compute, fit scaling exponents, test small-run extrapolation, or vary architecture shape. Other reported benchmark and ablation results do not test the listed versions. Figure 1's exact accuracy values are not recoverable from the text.
record.test_reason: The study's 'Scaling Law by Difficulty' concerns fine-tuning data volume and difficulty, not model or pretraining scale. None of the versions is tested. The study varies the size of a narrow template-generated synthetic fine-tuning set and the difficulty of the data, then reports AIME24 accuracy. It does not vary parameters, pretraining tokens or compute. It reports no held-out loss and fits no power law. V6 concerns downstream performance against model or pretraining scale or pretraining loss, so a narrow fine-tuning-set size effect is a related but different construct. V5's fine-tuning case is about the power-law form of loss, which is never measured or fitted here. The 'scaling law' name is borrowed, not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors claim performance follows a U-shaped curve in training-data difficulty. They say abundant low-difficulty synthetic data hurts and hard curated data helps. They also claim their SST template framework improves math reasoning accuracy and efficiency, e.g. +6.18 on GSM8K and +2.18 on AIME24 over the base model.
record.recipe_differences: This is a fine-tuning study of synthetic-data volume and difficulty using downstream accuracy, not the original held-out-loss scaling-law measurement or fixed-compute allocation procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcome depends on training-data difficulty and composition: increasing low-difficulty synthetic data is associated with worse AIME24 accuracy, while a smaller high-difficulty Open-R1 dataset is reported to do better.

fits_no_version.finding: Fine-tuning DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B on more template-generated, mostly low-difficulty synthetic math data (0k to 100k) lowers AIME24 accuracy. A curated, harder Open-R1 set is reported to score higher (30.48).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream reasoning accuracy after fine-tuning does not rise monotonically with fine-tuning data volume; low-difficulty synthetic data can degrade it (data difficulty versus quantity).

record.problems: The relevant scaling result is limited to a narrow fine-tuning and math-task setting. Figure 1's exact values and uncertainty are not stated in the supplied text. The Open-R1 and synthetic-data comparison changes data composition as well as volume, so it does not isolate volume alone.
record.rows_left_out: No other reported results were extracted: the remaining tables and ablations concern SST stages, prompting, or training components rather than the claim versions.

untested.parts: No held-out loss or sweep of parameters, tokens or compute.
The study fine-tunes but measures no loss and fits no power-law form, and covers no other modality.
No variation of model scale or pretraining loss. Table 1 compares 1.5B models only. A 7B point appears in the Fig. 1 legend but is not analysed.
No comparison of exponents or fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The 'U-shaped' curve is asserted but never shown with data across difficulty levels. The only evidence is a volume sweep of easy data plus one Open-R1 comparison. Fig. 1's numbers are not recoverable from the text.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss or parameter, token, or compute scaling sweep.
No small-run power-law fits or predictions of larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation or parameter/token scaling comparison.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or architecture at fixed parameter count.
The study uses text-model fine-tuning but does not test whether the same power-law form holds; it does not report held-out loss, other modalities, repeated data, or transfer.
Tests downstream accuracy against fine-tuning data amount and composition in a narrow math-task setting, not accuracy against model scale or pretraining loss generally.
No comparison of fitting choices or exponents, and no test of parameter-counting or training-schedule sensitivity.

rows.subject: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B
rows.operation_detail: Varied the amount of template-generated synthetic training data and measured AIME24 accuracy.
rows.locator: Fig. 1 and its caption; Method, “Scaling Law by Difficulty”
rows.note: The text states that accuracy consistently drops as dataset size increases from 0k to 100k, but the exact plotted values are not available in the supplied text.
rows.check: This measures AIME24 accuracy against fine-tuning set size (0k–100k) for template-generated synthetic data. That is neither model or pretraining scale nor pretraining loss, so it does not bear on V6, and it is not a loss power law (V5). The values are figure-only. The text says only that accuracy 'consistently drops'.

rows.subject: SST-Framework
rows.operation_detail: Compared the reported AIME24 outcome using a smaller, high-difficulty Open-R1 dataset with the larger synthetic-data setting.

conditions.value: about one-fifth of the synthetic set

rows.note: The prose says this smaller Open-R1-data experiment achieves a much higher score; Table 1 reports SST-Framework at 30.48 ± 2.60 on AIME24. The compared data compositions differ as well as their volumes.
rows.check: This compares data composition (curated Open-R1 vs synthetic), not scale, and no synthetic-data accuracy is given as a baseline. The 30.48 value is identical to the final SST-Framework result in Table 1, so it is unclear whether it is a plain Open-R1 fine-tune or the full SST method. Fig. 1's legend labels the Open-R1 run as 97k, while the text calls it about one-fifth of the synthetic volume, which is inconsistent. In Table 1 this row is the study's own method compared with baselines and should not be treated as a scaling result.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Template-generated synthetic fine-tuning data, with AIME24 accuracy measured as data volume increases
reader_labels.reason: Accuracy is stated to fall from 0k to 100k data (r1), contrary to a general expectation that downstream performance improves with scale. The smaller high-difficulty Open-R1 setting is also reported to score higher than the larger synthetic setting (r2).
